questions.stem: According to the laws of reflection, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured between the rays and the

options.text: normal at the point of incidence

questions.explanation: By definition both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are measured from the normal, the line drawn perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray strikes. If a ray makes 30 degrees with a mirror surface, its angle of incidence is 90 − 30 = 60 degrees.

distractorRationale.b: Angles measured from the surface are the complements of i and r, so using them gives an answer that is wrong by 90 degrees minus the value
distractorRationale.c: The principal axis only exists for curved mirrors and is not used to define i and r
distractorRationale.d: The normal depends on the orientation of the surface, so it is only vertical in the special case of a horizontal mirror

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the image formed by a plane mirror?

options.text: Real, inverted and the same size as the object
Virtual, erect and the same size as the object
Virtual, erect and smaller than the object
Real, erect and larger than the object

questions.explanation: The rays leaving a plane mirror only appear to come from a point behind it, so the image is virtual. It is the same way up as the object, so it is erect, and its magnification is exactly 1, so it is the same size. It is also laterally inverted, which is a left-to-right swap and not a turning upside down.

distractorRationale.a: A plane mirror image can never be caught on a screen, so it is not real, and it is erect rather than inverted
distractorRationale.c: Diminished images come from convex mirrors; a plane mirror always gives magnification 1
distractorRationale.d: A plane mirror never magnifies and never forms a real image

questions.stem: The image formed by a plane mirror can be caught on a white screen placed behind the mirror.
questions.explanation: False. No light actually reaches the position of the image — the reflected rays merely diverge as if they had started there. Since no light arrives at that point, a screen placed there stays dark. That is exactly what the word virtual means.

distractorRationale.a: Only real images, where light rays genuinely meet, can be caught on a screen. Plane mirror images are always virtual

questions.stem: A girl stands 2.0 m in front of a large plane mirror. Calculate the distance between the girl and her image. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: The image is formed as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, so it lies 2.0 m behind the glass. The girl and her image are therefore separated by $2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0\ \text{m}$. The common error is to answer 2.0 m, which is only the distance from the girl to the mirror.

questions.stem: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 24 cm. Calculate its focal length. Give your answer in centimetres.
questions.explanation: For a spherical mirror the focal length is half the radius of curvature: $f = \frac{r}{2} = \frac{24}{2} = 12\ \text{cm}$. Doubling instead of halving, which would give 48 cm, is the usual mistake.

questions.stem: A ray of light falls on a plane mirror. The mirror is rotated through 12° while the incident ray is kept fixed. Calculate the angle through which the reflected ray turns. Give your answer in degrees.
questions.explanation: Rotating the mirror through an angle also rotates the normal through the same angle, which changes the angle of incidence by that amount and the angle of reflection by the same amount again. The reflected ray therefore turns through twice the rotation of the mirror: $2 \times 12^\circ = 24^\circ$.

questions.stem: Two plane mirrors are inclined to each other at an angle of 60°. Calculate the number of images of a small object placed between them.
questions.explanation: The number of images formed by two inclined mirrors is $n = \frac{360}{\theta} - 1$. Here $\frac{360}{60} = 6$, so $n = 6 - 1 = 5$ images. Forgetting to subtract 1 gives the common wrong answer of 6.

questions.stem: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Calculate the distance of the image from the mirror. Give your answer in centimetres.
questions.explanation: From the mirror formula, $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{15} = \frac{3-2}{30} = \frac{1}{30}$, so $v = 30\ \text{cm}$. The positive value confirms a real image, formed 30 cm in front of the mirror. Since the object lies between F and C, the image is real, inverted and magnified.

questions.stem: An object 3.0 cm tall is placed 20 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Calculate the height of the image. Give your answer in centimetres.
questions.explanation: First find the image distance: $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{15} - \frac{1}{20} = \frac{4-3}{60} = \frac{1}{60}$, so $v = 60\ \text{cm}$. The magnification is $m = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{60}{20} = 3$. Image height $= m \times$ object height $= 3 \times 3.0 = 9.0\ \text{cm}$. The image is real, inverted and three times as tall as the object.

questions.stem: A convex mirror is preferred to a plane mirror as a driving mirror mainly because it

options.text: gives a wider field of view
forms a real image of the road behind

questions.explanation: Because a convex mirror diverges the light falling on it, rays from a very wide region behind the vehicle can reach the driver's eye from a small mirror. The image is always virtual, erect and diminished, and the diminished size is precisely what allows so much of the road to fit into the mirror.

distractorRationale.b: A convex mirror forms only virtual images, whatever the position of the object
distractorRationale.c: It diminishes rather than magnifies, which is why vehicles behind look further away than they really are
distractorRationale.d: Every plane and convex mirror image is laterally inverted; the curvature does not remove this

questions.stem: What is the focal length of a concave mirror if the radius of curvature is 30 cm?
questions.explanation: The focal length (f) of a concave mirror is half the radius of curvature (R). Therefore, f = R/2 = 30 cm / 2 = 15 cm. This relationship is fundamental in optics.

distractorRationale.b: This option confuses radius with focal length.
distractorRationale.c: This option incorrectly doubles the radius of curvature.
distractorRationale.d: This option is incorrect as it does not follow the formula for focal length.
